description: Carved, formerly polychromed zoomorphic spirit deity derived from a pig/boar. The face is long with bared teeth, large eyes and ears back. The tongue is outstretched and the stance is also stretched forward in the manner of the Mekekattu nandi deities. The body is small and rounded and there are rudimentary anklets on all four limbs just above the hoofs.

archive_metadata.condition_assessment: Severely damaged and cracked on the forehead and on the snout

interpretation.explanation: Panjurli is interpreted here as a boar-associated Bhuta figure. This reading connects the sculpture to protective and ritual functions, while remaining an interpretive layer rather than a definitive explanation.

recoloring.explanation: The recoloring is an interpretive prototype based on material color blocking. It is not presented as an exact historical reconstruction.

description: Carved, formerly polychromed form of a theriomorphic spirit deity, with the head of a Nandi atop a human physique. The male figure has a commanding appearance, a tall frame, broad shoulders, erect posture with legs apart. The head is weathered and no details other than the raised ears remain of the bovine face. The hands are at right angles to the chest with one of them holding the remnants of a shield or a club. The other arm looks like it might have held a weapon previously which is missing now.  There is a short chain at the neck with a oval pendant and a braided sacred thread falls diagonally across the chest. The lower garment has two folds and below it the clearly carved knees caps are visible. There are anklets around the ankles.

interpretation.explanation: Nandigona is interpreted here as an upright hybrid Bhuta figure with animal-associated features. In the recolored version, the dark red body, yellow ornaments, sash, and patterned lower garment emphasize its ritual and performative character. This reading connects the sculpture to protective and spirit-related functions, while remaining an interpretive layer rather than a definitive explanation.

recoloring.explanation: This sculpture can be used as a comparison for color choices, especially where polychromed surfaces are visible.

description: Sculpted, formerly polychromed form of the spirit deity, believed to be a mother goddess. She is seated in a typical posture, i.e. one leg folded across the saddle and another dropping down on one side. Her hair is tied onto one side, in a bun, one of the typical styles common to female deities. Both her arms are bent at right angles to her torso and the weapons she usually holds are missing. She is on her mount, a bull, called Akasa Nandi. A vestige of the wing (on the left side in this image) can be seen on the side of the bull.

archive_metadata.curatorial_note: The deity is placed in the sanctum sanctorum of the Mekekattu shrine. JVM ledger to be checked for further details of object.
archive_metadata.condition_assessment: Visible damages to the wood, treated(?)

interpretation.type: female deity figure with animal mount
interpretation.meaning: female divine presence / mounted spirit form
interpretation.explanation: Ammanavaru is interpreted here as a female Bhuta or goddess-associated figure shown with an animal mount or support. In the recolored version, the red-brown body, green upper garment, yellow lower garment, bright ornaments, and animal form below emphasize both human-like presence and ritual display. This reading connects the sculpture to protection, devotion, and local spirit traditions, while remaining an interpretive layer rather than a definitive explanation.
